```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5,
                      dpi = 72, out.width = "100%")
has_cub <- requireNamespace("CUB", quietly = TRUE)
```

A **flower plot** shows all the distributions observed on a unit as the
petals of a flower. Each variable is a stem going from the centre outwards;
along the stem the distance from the centre is the value (its position in the
range of the variable, as in the other plots of the package), and at each value
a petal opens sideways, with a width proportional to its probability and the
colour of the value.

A Green Eyes plot and a flower plot of the same unit show the same
information in two ways: in the eye the radius is the *cumulative*
probability, so that the eye is good at showing levels (the median, the share
of low or high values); in the flower the radius is the *value*, so that the
flower shows the *shape* of the distributions: modes, gaps, long tails.

```{r}
library(DistrViz)
library(DDAWASS)
```

## Discrete distributions: one petal for each value

```{r, eval = has_cub}
data(univer, package = "CUB")
univer$Faculty <- factor(sprintf("F%02d", univer$faculty))
univer$Gender  <- factor(univer$gender, levels = 0:1, labels = c("M", "W"))
items <- c("informat", "willingn", "officeho", "compete", "global")
dv <- dv_data(univer, unit = c("Faculty", "Gender"), vars = items, support = 1:7,
              min.n = 10)
```

For discrete distributions each support value is an elliptic petal. The
white dots (`show_median = TRUE`) mark the medians; the sectors are ordered by
the shortest Hamiltonian cycle through the variables (`var_order = "tsp"`, see
`dv_var_order()`), as in the Green Eyes plots.

```{r, eval = has_cub, fig.width = 5, fig.height = 5, out.width = "65%", fig.align = "center"}
flower_plot(dv, row = "F13_M", var_order = "tsp", show_median = TRUE)
```

The flower of F13_M has petals all along the stems: the ratings of this group
are spread over the whole scale, with a visible share of 1s and 2s (the red
petals near the centre). Compare it with the most satisfied groups, whose
flowers open only at the top of the stems:

```{r, eval = has_cub, fig.height = 2.9}
flower_grid(dv, rows = c("F02_W", "F07_M", "F09_M", "F13_M"), var_order = "tsp",
            ncol = 4)
```

The flower of F07_M is a good example of what a flower shows better than an
eye: in the office hours (`officeho`) the petals are spread over all the scale,
a polarised distribution, while the other aspects have a single mode at the
top.

By default the widths of the petals are comparable across units (the widest
petal of all the drawn units has the width `petal_width`, a fraction of the
half-sector); with `width_scale = "unit"` each flower uses its own largest
petal. Flowers can be grouped or ordered by a clustering as in `gei_grid()`:

```{r, eval = has_cub, fig.height = 8.5}
hc <- WD_hclust(dv$source, method = "ward.D2")
flower_grid(dv, groups = cutree(hc, 3), var_order = "tsp", ncol = 6)
```

## Flowers on the factorial plane

`flower_pca()` is the flower version of `gei_pca()` (see the vignette on Green
Eyes plots): each flower is drawn at the position of its unit on the first
factorial plane of the quantile-based MFA (`DDAWASS::WD.MultiplePCA()`), the
outline is coloured by a partition and the key on the right is the flower of
the barycenter of all the units, with the names of the variables. Any matrix
of coordinates can be given instead of the factorial analysis, also with a map
in the background (see the vignette on flower plots of histogram data).

```{r, eval = has_cub, fig.height = 5}
flower_pca(dv, var_order = "tsp", groups = cutree(hc, 3), size = 0.15, key_size = 0.5)
```

## Style

The original design has a black background, a green receptacle and orange
sepals. `style = "light"` gives a white background and `center = "plain"` a
grey centre; any palette of `dv_palette()` can be used.

```{r, eval = has_cub, fig.height = 2.9}
flower_grid(dv, rows = c("F02_W", "F07_M", "F09_M", "F13_M"), var_order = "tsp",
            ncol = 4, style = "light", center = "plain", palette = "Hiroshige")
```

## Histograms: violin petals

For histograms the petals of the classes are joined into a violin whose
width follows the density. The histograms are discretized into `n_levels`
classes (30 by default for flower plots) and the profile of the violins is
smoothed with a Gaussian kernel (`smooth`, in classes; the colours are not
smoothed).

```{r, fig.height = 5.5}
flower_grid(HistDAWass::BLOOD, rows = 1:6, ncol = 3, palette = "Zissou 1",
            labels = TRUE)
```

The monthly temperatures of a station of the `China_Month` data make a
flower with twelve petals; with a common scale for all the months
(`scheme = "global"`) the petals move outwards in summer and inwards in
winter, and their width shows the variability of each month across the
years.

```{r, fig.width = 5.5, fig.height = 5.5, out.width = "70%", fig.align = "center"}
library(HistDAWass)
Temp <- China_Month[, match(paste0("mean.temp_", month.abb), colnames(China_Month@M))]
colnames(Temp@M) <- month.abb
rownames(Temp@M) <- sub("_[0-9]+$", "", rownames(Temp@M))
flower_plot(Temp, row = "HaErBin", n_levels = 60, scheme = "global",
            palette = "Blue-Red 3", style = "light")
```
